title: Power Markets & Market Design
summary:
Electricity is a commodity unlike any other: it can barely be stored, and supply must match demand **every instant** or the grid frequency drifts and the system collapses. That single fact shapes the whole market. Instead of one price, there is a **sequence of markets** running from years ahead down to real time, each one a chance to re-balance your position as forecasts sharpen.

The backbone is the **merit order**. At any moment, every available generator is ranked by its **short-run marginal cost (SRMC)** — the cost of producing one more MWh, dominated by fuel and CO$_2$ costs. Cheap-to-run plants (wind, solar, nuclear, run-of-river) sit at the left; expensive peakers (open-cycle gas, oil) at the right. The market stacks them up until supply meets demand, and the **last unit needed — the marginal unit — sets the price for everyone**. This is **marginal (pay-as-clear) pricing**: a wind farm that bid €0 still earns the clearing price set by, say, a gas plant. The gap between the clearing price and a plant's own SRMC is its **inframarginal rent** — how it recovers fixed and capital costs.

The **market timeline** has four main stages. **Forward / futures** markets (years to days ahead) let players hedge price risk financially. The **day-ahead market** is the main event: a single daily auction (in Europe, coupled across borders via **EPEX SPOT** and **Nord Pool** into one big optimisation, SDAC/EUPHEMIA) clears 24 hourly prices for tomorrow. The **intraday market** runs continuously after that, letting participants trade out forecast errors as the delivery hour approaches (gate closure). Finally the **balancing market** is the TSO's real-time tool: it activates reserves (FCR, aFRR, mFRR) to fix the residual mismatch, and the resulting **imbalance price** penalises anyone who deviated from their schedule.

Because renewables have near-zero SRMC, adding wind and solar pushes the whole merit order to the right — the **merit-order effect** — lowering average wholesale prices but also producing **negative prices** when must-run and subsidised output exceeds demand and it is cheaper to pay to keep running than to shut down. Two more market layers fix what energy-only pricing misses: **capacity markets** pay generators to *be available* (resource adequacy), and **ancillary-services / balancing markets** pay for the frequency control, reserves and voltage support that keep the system stable. Spanning bidding zones, **interconnectors** and **market coupling** let cheap power flow to expensive zones until a line **congests**, at which point prices split between zones. For long-term hedging and financing renewables, buyers and generators increasingly sign **Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs)** at a fixed price, sidestepping the spot market's volatility.

The analyst's core reflex: to explain or forecast a price, **find the marginal unit** and compute its SRMC; to judge a gas plant's economics, look at the **spark spread**; to read a renewables-heavy market, watch the **residual load** (demand minus wind and solar) — it is what the dispatchable fleet and the price actually respond to.

equations.name: Short-run marginal cost (SRMC)
equations.useWhen: Estimating the price-setting bid of a thermal plant. The day-ahead market clears at the SRMC of the **marginal unit**, so this *is* the wholesale price when a given plant is on the margin.
equations.note: $P_{fuel}$ in €/MWh$_{th}$ (per MWh of *fuel*), $\eta$ the electrical efficiency, $e_f$ the fuel's CO$_2$ intensity (t/MWh$_{th}$), $P_{CO_2}$ the carbon price (€/t), $VOM$ variable O&M. Dividing by $\eta$ converts fuel-side costs to per-MWh-electricity.

equations.name: Spark spread
equations.useWhen: The gross margin of a **gas** plant per MWh of electricity, before carbon. A positive spark spread means it is profitable to run; the sign flips a plant in or out of the merit order.
equations.note: Ignores CO$_2$. The 'dark spread' is the same idea for a coal plant ($P_{coal}$ instead of $P_{gas}$).

equations.name: Clean spark spread
equations.useWhen: The *true* gas-plant margin once the cost of emission allowances is included. Comparing the clean spark spread to the clean dark spread tells you whether gas or coal is 'in the money' — the fuel-switching dynamic that drives emissions.
equations.note: Subtract the carbon term from the plain spark spread. A high CO$_2$ price lifts the clean spark spread above the clean dark spread, pushing coal down the merit order.

equations.name: Marginal (pay-as-clear) settlement
equations.useWhen: Settling a uniform-price auction: *every* accepted seller is paid the single clearing price, not their own bid. Use the rent form to see how a near-zero-cost unit (wind, nuclear) earns margin to cover fixed costs.
equations.note: Contrast with **pay-as-bid**, where each unit is paid its own offer. Pay-as-clear is the European day-ahead standard and rewards honest marginal-cost bidding.

equations.name: Residual load
equations.useWhen: Reading a renewables-heavy market. The dispatchable fleet and the price respond to *residual* load, not gross demand — low or negative residual load is when negative prices and curtailment appear.
equations.note: $L$ is total demand. Also called 'net load'. The classic 'duck curve' is the daily shape of residual load as solar swings.

glossary.definition: The ranking of generators by **short-run marginal cost**, from cheapest to most expensive. The market dispatches up the stack until supply meets demand.
The last (most expensive) generator needed to meet demand. Its SRMC sets the single clearing price paid to *all* accepted sellers.
A uniform-price auction: everyone who clears is paid the price of the marginal unit, regardless of their own bid. The European day-ahead standard.
Alternative settlement where each accepted seller receives its own offered price. Encourages strategic bidding rather than honest marginal cost.
Cost of generating one more MWh now — mainly fuel/efficiency plus CO$_2$ cost plus variable O&M. The bid a rational plant submits.
Clearing price minus a plant's own SRMC, times its output. How cheap-to-run plants (wind, nuclear) recover fixed and capital costs under marginal pricing.
The main daily auction: one round clears 24 hourly (or quarter-hourly) prices for the next day. In Europe, coupled across borders into a single optimisation.
Continuous trading after the day-ahead auction, up to **gate closure**, used to correct forecast errors (e.g. a wind shortfall) close to delivery.
The TSO's real-time mechanism: it activates reserves to match the final supply–demand mismatch and prices the imbalance back to those who deviated.
The price a party pays (or receives) for deviating from its scheduled position, derived from the cost of the balancing energy the TSO had to activate.
The cut-off time after which schedules are fixed and only the TSO (via balancing) can act. Marks the handover from market to system operation.
The marketplaces that run day-ahead and intraday auctions for electricity. EPEX SPOT covers Central-West Europe; Nord Pool the Nordics/Baltics and beyond.
The algorithm that clears coupled European day-ahead markets together, using interconnector capacity to equalise prices between zones as far as the grid allows.
A geographic area with a single wholesale price, within which grid congestion is assumed negligible. Prices differ *between* zones when links congest.
A transmission link between bidding zones (often an HVDC cable). Lets cheap power flow to expensive zones until the line hits its capacity limit.
When a transmission line cannot carry all the power the market wants to send across it. Forces prices to **split** between the constrained zones.
Wholesale prices below zero, occurring when inflexible must-run and subsidised output exceeds demand: it is cheaper to pay to keep generating than to shut down and restart.
The downward push on average wholesale prices from adding near-zero-cost wind and solar, which displace expensive plants and shift the marginal unit leftward.
Demand minus wind and solar output — the load the dispatchable fleet must serve. Drives prices, ramping needs and curtailment more than gross demand.
A mechanism that pays generators (and demand response) to *be available* at peak, ensuring resource adequacy that an energy-only market may under-reward.
Grid-stability products bought by the TSO: frequency reserves (FCR, aFRR, mFRR), voltage/reactive support, black-start — distinct from selling energy.
Frequency reserves by speed: **FCR** (Frequency Containment, seconds, arrests the drop), **aFRR** (automatic restoration), **mFRR** (manual restoration, minutes).
A gas plant's gross margin per MWh of electricity: power price minus gas cost adjusted for efficiency. The 'clean' version also subtracts the CO$_2$ cost.
A long-term contract to buy power at a pre-agreed price. **Physical** (delivers energy), **financial/virtual** (a price hedge as a contract-for-difference). Key to financing renewables.
**Dispatchable** plants can be ramped on demand (gas, hydro); **variable** renewables follow weather; **must-run** units (some CHP, nuclear) cannot easily switch off, contributing to negative prices.
Letting prices spike toward the cap when reserves run short, signalling the value of capacity and demand response. The energy-only alternative to a capacity market.

tips: **To explain any wholesale price, find the marginal unit.** The clearing price ≈ the SRMC of the last plant dispatched. Gas on the margin ⇒ price tracks gas + CO$_2$; renewables on the margin ⇒ price near zero.
**Divide fuel-side costs by efficiency.** A €30/MWh$_{th}$ gas price at $\eta = 0.5$ costs €60/MWh$_{el}$. Forgetting the $1/\eta$ is the most common SRMC and spark-spread mistake.
**Pay-as-clear ≠ pay-as-bid.** In the European day-ahead market everyone is paid the *clearing* price, so a €0-bid wind farm still earns the gas-set price — that margin is its inframarginal rent.

**Negative prices are a flexibility signal, not an error.** They appear when residual load is very low and must-run/subsidised output can't switch off. They reward storage, interconnection and flexible demand.

**Watch residual load, not demand.** In a renewables-heavy zone the dispatchable fleet and the price respond to demand *minus* wind and solar — that is where ramping, curtailment and price swings come from.

**Clean spark vs clean dark spread = fuel switching.** When a rising CO$_2$ price lifts the clean spark spread above the clean dark spread, gas undercuts coal in the merit order and emissions fall — a core decarbonisation lever.
